science.title: We may need a new map to properly interpret our genome
science.description: Genetic information may play an increasingly important role in the personalized preventive medicine of the future. Whole-genome sequencing could open up new possibilities for identifying susceptibility to and risk of specific diseases even before symptoms appear, emphasizes Dr. Gyula Richárd Nagy, a clinical geneticist at Semmelweis University. However, to achieve this, we must first accurately "read" our genome—that is, the billions of DNA letters—with increasing precision. We must also ensure that the reference we are comparing it to is appropriate.

science.title: First global genome atlas reveals overlooked microscopic life in hundreds of lakes and reservoirs
science.description: Tiny single-celled organisms help keep lakes clear, but some can also contaminate the water. An international research team has analyzed DNA data from 362 lakes to create the first global genome atlas of these organisms. With the findings now published in Nature Communications, the new atlas lays the foundation for faster and more precise monitoring of lakes.

science.title: High-density SNP mapping reveals genomic hotspots for photosynthetic traits under Huanglongbing disease in citrus
science.description: Huanglongbing (HLB) is a major constraint to citrus production, but the genetic basis of physiological responses to Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (CLas) infection remains poorly understood. Here, we characterized photosynthetic and gas-exchange responses and investigated their genetic architecture in 120 F₁ hybrids derived from ‘Daisy’ tangerine × Carrizo citrange. Hybrids were evaluated before HLB infection and across four subsequent assessment periods following artificial CLas exposure. Fifteen physiological and environmental traits were measured and CLas infection was confirmed in all F₁ hybrids by quantitative real-time PCR. HLB-associated physiological responses were characterized by declines in net photosynthetic rate, stomatal conductance, transpiration and intercellular CO2 flux, accompanied by increased intercellular CO2 concentration and vapour pressure deficit. Multivariate analysis indicated that gas exchange and water relations constituted the major sources of phenotypic variation, with the first three principal components explaining 81.81% of the total variation. High broad-sense heritability and genetic advance were observed for several key traits, particularly stomatal conductance, intercellular CO2 flux, net photosynthetic rate, transpiration and vapour pressure deficit, indicating substantial genetic variation for these responses. High-density parental SNP linkage maps were subsequently used for QTL analysis. Twenty-six QTLs were detected on the ‘Daisy’ tangerine map and 28 on the Carrizo citrange map, with individual loci explaining 10.6–17.8% of phenotypic variance. Several QTLs were repeatedly detected across seasons and overlapping loci were identified for physiologically related traits. These stable genomic regions provide useful targets for validation and further dissection of the genetic basis of physiological responses under HLB infection.
